body:
Why preparedness is essential

Scientists can identify earthquake-prone regions and monitor seismic activity, but they cannot reliably predict the exact date, time, location and magnitude of a future major earthquake sufficiently in advance for ordinary public planning.

Consequently, earthquake preparedness must be maintained continuously rather than undertaken only after a specific prediction or rumour.

Preparedness includes safer surroundings, awareness of appropriate protective action, household emergency arrangements and regular practice.

Before an earthquake

Households, schools and workplaces can reduce avoidable injuries through basic precautions.

  • Identify relatively safe places where occupants can protect themselves from falling or flying objects.
  • Secure heavy cupboards, shelves, water heaters and other items that could fall.
  • Keep exits and passages clear of unnecessary obstructions.
  • Prepare essential emergency supplies such as drinking water, necessary medicines, a torch, basic first-aid materials and important contact information.
  • Establish a family communication and meeting plan in case members become separated.
  • Learn the locations of relevant utility controls so that gas, electricity or other supplies can be shut off safely if required.
  • Practise appropriate earthquake-safety drills in homes, schools and workplaces.

People with disabilities, older persons, children and others requiring assistance should be included in household and institutional preparedness arrangements.

During shaking: Drop, Cover and Hold On

When an earthquake begins while a person is indoors, the generally recommended protective action is Drop, Cover and Hold On.

  1. Drop: Get down onto hands and knees to reduce the chance of being knocked over.
  2. Cover: Protect the head and neck, preferably beneath a sturdy desk or table. If such shelter is unavailable, move as little as possible to a safer position away from falling hazards and protect the head and neck with the arms.
  3. Hold On: Hold onto the shelter, or maintain protective positioning, until the shaking stops.

Remain indoors during the shaking if already inside. Running outdoors while the ground is moving can expose a person to falling glass, masonry and other debris. Avoid windows, tall unsecured furniture and objects likely to fall.

Do not use elevators. Doorways are not generally safer than other parts of modern buildings, and standing in a doorway is not a substitute for protecting the head and neck.

When outdoors or travelling

If already outdoors, remain outside and move to a clear area away from buildings, trees, electric lines and other overhead hazards when it is safe to do so. Protect yourself from falling or flying objects.

If travelling in a vehicle, the driver should pull over safely away from bridges, flyovers, buildings and overhead wires, stop and remain in the vehicle until the shaking ends. The vehicle should not be stopped beneath structures that may fall.

The correct response depends on the person's immediate surroundings. The general objective is to avoid falls, falling objects and unstable structures without creating additional danger through unnecessary movement.

After the shaking stops

The end of the main shaking does not mean that every danger has disappeared. Aftershocks may follow the main earthquake, and damaged buildings can remain unstable.

  • Check for injuries and seek appropriate medical assistance where necessary.
  • Move away from visibly damaged or unstable structures when it is safe to do so.
  • Use stairs rather than lifts when evacuating a building after shaking has stopped and the route is safe.
  • Avoid fallen power lines, damaged electrical installations, gas leaks and other obvious hazards.
  • Do not enter or re-enter a seriously damaged building until it has been assessed and declared safe by competent authorities or professionals.
  • Follow verified information and instructions issued by relevant public authorities.
  • Remain prepared to repeat protective action if another tremor occurs.

A person should not operate damaged electrical or gas equipment or attempt repairs when doing so may be dangerous. Unsafe utilities should be dealt with by competent personnel.

Preparedness in schools and communities

Schools should identify suitable protective spaces, practise earthquake drills, keep routes clear and establish arrangements for accounting for students and staff after the shaking ends.

At community level, preparedness includes awareness programmes, communication arrangements, identification of vulnerable residents and coordination with local disaster-management authorities.

Regular drills help convert knowledge into familiar behaviour. However, drills do not replace the need for structurally safe buildings.

Prelims focus

  • Reliable prediction of the exact time and location of a future major earthquake is not presently possible.
  • Drop, Cover and Hold On is the recommended protective action for most indoor situations during shaking.
  • People already indoors should not rush outside while shaking continues.
  • People outdoors should stay clear of buildings, trees and overhead electric lines.
  • Aftershocks and damaged structures remain hazards after the main shaking stops.
  • Trap: Running to a doorway or using a lift is not the recommended general indoor response.

[References: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 194–195, 2018–19 printing; National Disaster Management Authority, Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapter 6, Awareness and Preparedness, pp. 29–31; Directorate General Fire Services, Civil Defence and Home Guards, Ministry of Home Affairs, Earthquakes, section What to Do During an Earthquake, accessed 2 November 2026; U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Safety Guidelines: During an Earthquake, section Drop, Cover and Hold On, accessed 2 November 2026.]

body:
Earthquake management requires several institutions

Earthquake-risk reduction cannot be achieved by a single department. It requires scientific monitoring, hazard assessment, building standards, enforcement, public preparedness and coordinated disaster management.

Different institutions perform different functions. A common error is to confuse organisations that study earthquakes with those responsible for building regulation or disaster-management administration.

Important institutions and their roles

InstitutionPrincipal role
GSDMAState-level disaster management, mitigation, preparedness and coordination of recovery.
NDMANational disaster-management policies and guidelines, including earthquake-risk reduction.
ISR, GujaratSeismological research, earthquake monitoring, hazard assessment and microzonation.
NCSNational seismic monitoring, earthquake detection and dissemination of earthquake information.
BISDevelopment and publication of technical standards, including earthquake-resistant construction standards.
GIDMDisaster-management training, education and capacity building in Gujarat.
District and local authoritiesLocal disaster-management planning, public coordination and enforcement of applicable building regulations through competent authorities.

Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) was established on 8 February 2001, shortly after the Bhuj earthquake. It initially coordinated earthquake rehabilitation and reconstruction and subsequently developed a wider role covering disaster prevention, mitigation, preparedness and management.

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003 provides the state's statutory disaster-management framework. Under Section 7, the Chief Minister of Gujarat is the ex-officio chairperson of GSDMA. Other members include 2 ministers nominated by the Chief Minister; the Chief Secretary, Revenue Secretary, Chief Executive Officer of GSDMA, State Relief Commissioner and Director General of Police, ex officio; and any other state officers appointed by the State Government.

At the district level, the district administration and disaster-management institutions undertake local planning and coordination. This is important because the effects of an earthquake differ between settlements and require locally appropriate action.

Scientific monitoring and hazard assessment

The Institute of Seismological Research (ISR) in Gujarat studies earthquake processes and regional seismic hazards. Its activities include earthquake monitoring, fault studies, site-specific hazard assessment and seismic microzonation.

The National Centre for Seismology (NCS), under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, operates the National Seismological Network and provides earthquake information.

Seismic monitoring detects and characterises earthquake activity. It should not be confused with a reliable prediction of exactly when a future major earthquake will occur.

Hazard maps and microzonation studies help authorities identify potentially dangerous locations, prioritise mitigation and support safer development decisions.

Training, regulation and public preparedness

The Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management (GIDM) supports disaster-management education and capacity building. Training is important because plans and technical standards are effective only when the relevant people understand their responsibilities.

Urban local bodies and development authorities play an important part in applying building regulations. BIS provides technical standards, while the competent regulatory authorities administer building approvals, inspections and enforcement under applicable law.

At the community level, households, schools and local organisations contribute through preparedness drills, safer surroundings and awareness of public precautions.

How earthquake-risk reduction works as a complete system

Earthquake-risk management combines activities undertaken before, during and after an event.

  • Risk identification: Understand seismic hazards, exposed settlements and vulnerable buildings.
  • Prevention and mitigation: Use suitable land-use decisions, safer construction and retrofitting to reduce probable losses.
  • Preparedness: Develop plans, conduct drills and prepare communication and public-awareness arrangements.
  • Response: Coordinate protective public action, emergency assistance and essential services following an earthquake.
  • Recovery: Restore housing, livelihoods, infrastructure and community functioning while reducing earlier vulnerabilities.

Prevention does not mean stopping tectonic earthquakes from occurring. In this context, preventive and mitigation measures aim to avoid creating unnecessary exposure and to reduce damage when shaking occurs.

The central lesson of the 2001 earthquake: Earthquake hazard cannot be eliminated, but much of the resulting disaster risk can be reduced through scientific assessment, safer buildings, institutional preparedness and informed public action.

Integrated revision of Gujarat earthquake risk

The important connections are straightforward. Kachchh is a major intraplate seismic region. Its earthquake history demonstrates the continuing presence of the hazard. The scale of destruction in 2001 reflected not only powerful shaking but also the vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure.

Seismic zonation identifies broad regional hazard, while microzonation provides more detailed local information. Indian Standards provide technical guidance for safer construction, and competent authorities are responsible for applying relevant regulatory requirements.

Existing vulnerable structures may need professional assessment and seismic retrofitting. Schools, hospitals and essential infrastructure deserve special attention because their failure affects wider community safety.

Finally, everyday preparedness remains necessary even in places where major earthquakes are infrequent. Correct protective action during shaking and sensible precautions afterwards can reduce avoidable injuries.

Prelims focus

  • GSDMA was established on 8 February 2001 after the Gujarat earthquake.
  • The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2003.
  • The Chief Minister is the ex-officio chairperson of GSDMA under Section 7 of the state Act.
  • ISR studies earthquakes and conducts seismic hazard assessment in Gujarat.
  • BIS develops earthquake-related standards; competent state and local authorities enforce applicable building regulations.
  • Trap: Earthquake monitoring, seismic prediction, building-code enforcement and disaster-response coordination are different functions.

[References: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Constitution and History, sections on establishment and composition of the Authority, accessed 2 November 2026; Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management, Introduction, sections on the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act and institutional development, page updated 17 September 2026; Institute of Seismological Research, Mission and Seismic Hazard Assessment and Microzonation Group, accessed 2 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, National Framework for Structural Safety Audits and Seismic Resilience of Buildings, 23 July 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapters 2–6.]
